# ======================================================
# 📌 Introduction to R and Data Handling in RStudio
# ======================================================

There is lots of syntax to learn for working in R. A lot of this will come in time, with practice, and trial and error. Here are some basics to get you started.

Remember learning R is like learning a language. It will get easier, in time.

::: {.callout-important}
## How to use this tutorial

The gray boxes below are **live R editors** — the code actually runs in your browser (no install needed). In the top-left corner of each gray box, you'll see a **green arrow button labeled "Run Code."** Click that green arrow to run the code in that box. The output (whatever the code produces — a number, a table, a plot, etc.) will appear directly underneath the box a moment later.

You can also edit the code first — click inside the box, change something, then click the green **Run Code** arrow to run your edited version. Nothing you do here can break anything; if you make a mess, just refresh the page to start that box over.

Some sections are marked **🧠 Your Turn**. Those give you a task and a blank (or partially blank) code editor. Try to write the code yourself before you look at the answer — the solution is hidden underneath in a collapsed box. Click it open only after you've given it a real attempt (or if you're truly stuck).

**A note on browser vs. RStudio code:** Starting in Part 2, a few chunks run automatically in the background (you'll see them labeled `#| autorun: true`). These chunks fetch the data files from the web so they're available in your browser — you don't need to do anything with them. **When you write your own scripts in RStudio, you will not include this fetching code.** Immediately after each autorun chunk, you'll find a green box labeled **"In your RStudio script"** showing the simpler code you'll actually use.
:::

# 🛠 1. Basic R Concepts

There are lots of amazing resources on using R on the web! Don't be shy about exploring these.

The following text is excerpted from [this resource](https://www.dataquest.io/blog/tutorial-getting-started-with-r-and-rstudio/#tve-jump-173bb2584fe):

> "Let's start off by introducing some features of the Console. The Console is a tab in RStudio where we can run R code.
>
> Notice that the window pane where the console is located contains three tabs: Console, Terminal and Jobs (this may vary depending on the version of RStudio in use). We'll focus on the Console for now.
>
> When we open RStudio, the console contains information about the version of R we're working with."

Below, instead of typing into RStudio's console, you can just type directly into the editors on this page and click **Run Code**.

## Assignment Operator (`<-`)

```{webr-r}
x <- 10  # Assigns the value 10 to x

print(x)  # Prints x

x  # Also prints x
```

## Creating a Simple Data Frame

We can read a data frame into R, but we can also create a data frame within R itself.

The following code creates a data frame called `my_data`:

```{webr-r}
my_data <- data.frame(name = c("Alice", "Bob"), age = c(25, 30))

print(my_data)
```

The data frame has two variables (columns): `name` and `age`. It has two rows, each corresponding to one person.

## Accessing Columns in a Data Frame (`$`)

We may want to view a particular column in the data frame, or, later when we start conducting analyses, refer to a particular variable. We do this using the `$` sign.

```{webr-r}
# Extracts the "name" column
my_data$name
```

## Indexing Rows and Columns `[row, column]`

We can also use R's indexing system to refer to a particular row or column.

```{webr-r}
my_data[1, 2]  # First row, second column
my_data[, 1]   # First column (all rows)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Your Turn" collapse="false"}
Using `my_data`, write one line of code that returns **Bob's age** using `$`-and-indexing together (i.e., pull the `age` column, then index the second element).
:::

```{webr-r}
# Your code here

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Solution — click to reveal"}
```{webr-r}
my_data$age[2]
```

**How this works, piece by piece:**

* `my_data$age` pulls out the entire `age` column from `my_data` — this returns a vector of all the ages, in row order: `25 30` (Alice's age, then Bob's age).
* `[2]` then indexes into that vector and grabs its **2nd element** — since Bob is in the 2nd row of `my_data`, this returns his age, `30`.
* Put together, `my_data$age[2]` reads as "give me the `age` column, then give me the 2nd value in it."

This combination — `$` to grab a column, then `[ ]` to grab a specific position within it — comes up constantly in R, so it's worth being comfortable with both steps individually before chaining them together.
:::

# ======================================================
# 📁 2. A Note on Project Organization
# ======================================================

In RStudio, we need a reliable way to tell R where to find (and save) files. You'll sometimes see older code use `setwd("C:/Users/yourname/YourFolder")` to do this — but **this course does not use `setwd()` as the standard workflow**. A path like that is tied to one specific computer and breaks the moment the project moves to a different machine (including, for grading, yours to mine).

Instead, this course uses an **RStudio Project** with a standard folder structure, set up once in the C01 reproducible-workflow assignment:

```
EOH635_project/
├── EOH635_project.Rproj
├── data_raw/          <- original files exactly as you received them (never edit these by hand)
├── data_processed/    <- new files your scripts create (cleaned, merged, recoded data)
├── scripts/           <- your .R / .qmd / .Rmd files
└── outputs/           <- tables, figures, and other generated results
```

When you open `EOH635_project.Rproj`, RStudio automatically sets your working directory to the project root — no `setwd()` needed. From there, you use **relative paths**, typically with `file.path()`, so the same script works on any computer:

```r
read.csv(file.path("data_raw", "class_data_raw.csv"))
```

For this lab, that means: Please put `class_data_raw.csv`, `PHL_NDVI_summer_annual.csv`, and `codebook.xlsx` in `data_raw/`, and save anything you create (like the merged dataset at the end of this lab) into `data_processed/`.

**In this browser-based tutorial, there's no local file system to point to at all** — the data files are fetched automatically for you from the web when you load Parts 2 and 3 of this lesson, using the same `data_raw` / `data_processed` folder names so the code you see here matches what you'll type in RStudio.

**This is important to keep straight:** the "fetch from the web" step you'll see in Parts 2 and 3 is a workaround that exists *only* on these tutorial pages, because your browser has no access to any files at all — not the tutorial's, and not yours. **For your actual project, the data will live as real files on your own computer**, saved into the `data_raw/` folder of the `EOH635_project` you set up in RStudio. Your project scripts will simply read those files directly off your hard drive with `read.csv(file.path("data_raw", "..."))` — no downloading, no internet fetch, no `data_base_url`. Every time this tutorial shows a "fetch from the web" step, look for the green **"In your RStudio script"** box right after it — that box shows the shorter, simpler line you'll actually use for your project.

# ======================================================
# 📦 3. Loading Required Packages
# ======================================================

[This](https://faculty.washington.edu/kenrice/rintro/sess08.pdf) is a great tutorial on packages in R.

Briefly (quoting from that guide):

> "Base R includes pre-installed packages that allow for a fully functioning statistical environment in which a variety of analyses can be conducted. Thousands of user-contributed extension packages are available that provide enhanced functionality with R.
>
> R packages are collections of functions, data, and compiled code in a well-defined format.
>
> In order to install an extension package, we can invoke the `install.packages()` function, which typically downloads the package from CRAN and installs it for use."

You only need to install a package one time on your computer (upon first use, or after installing/re-installing/updating R). After installing it, you need to *load* it every session with `library()`.

On your own computer you'd run:

```r
install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
```

::: {.callout-note}
This tutorial page has already installed and loaded **tidyverse** for you in the background (that's what the `webr: packages:` setting in this page does). You can still call `library(tidyverse)` yourself below — it won't hurt anything, it's just already done.
:::

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## 💻 In your RStudio script

**This automatic install/load is unique to this tutorial page — it will not happen on your own computer.** `tidyverse` is actually a bundle of several packages (including `dplyr` and `tidyr`, which you'll use a lot), but the browser installing it silently for you is just a convenience built into this page.

When you write your own project scripts in RStudio, **you are responsible for installing and loading every package your code uses.** For any package (`tidyverse` or otherwise):

```r
install.packages("tidyverse")  # run this once per computer, the first time you use the package
library(tidyverse)              # run this at the top of every script/session that uses it
```

If you forget the `library()` line, R will give you an error like `could not find function "mutate"` (or whatever function you tried to use) — that's your signal to go back and load the package first.
:::
